metric_identity.metric_name: AI Adoption Rates by Industry — Sector-by-sector breakdown of enterprise AI and GenAI adoption from McKinsey Global Surveys (2024-2025)
metric_identity.source_report: McKinsey & Company / QuantumBlack 'The State of AI' Global Survey series: (1) 'The State of AI in Early 2024' (May 2024); (2) 'How Organizations Are Rewiring to Capture Value' (March 2025); (3) 'Agents, Innovation, and Transformation' (November 2025). Supplemented by GPTZero 'AI Adoption by Industry' analysis (2025), WalkMe '50 AI Adoption Statistics' (2025), and US Census Bureau data via St. Louis Fed.
metric_identity.publication_date: May 2024 (early 2024 survey); March 2025 and November 2025 (2025 survey editions)
metric_identity.methodology_notes: McKinsey 2024 survey: online survey in field February 22 to March 5, 2024, with 1,363 respondents across regions, industries, company sizes, functional specialties, and tenures; 981 confirmed AI adoption in at least one function, 878 regularly using GenAI. McKinsey 2025 survey: online survey June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 participants across 105 nations. Data weighted by contribution of each respondent's nation to global GDP. Supplementary industry-specific data from GPTZero aggregates US Census Bureau surveys, Salesforce State of Sales reports, and industry-specific studies. Self-reported survey data in all cases.

metric_value.value: Overall adoption: 78% of organizations using AI in at least one function (mid-2024), rising to 88% (mid-2025). GenAI-specific: 65% regularly using GenAI (early 2024), rising to 71-72% (mid-2025). By industry sector — Leading adopters: Technology, media & telecommunications (highest adoption, most AI agent deployment), Financial services/Insurance (adoption on par with technology sector by 2025), Healthcare (among top 3 for AI agent deployment). Function-level adoption: IT (18.1% highest single-function share), Marketing & Sales (43% of salespeople using AI in 2024, up from 24% in 2023), Service Operations (top 3 function). Manufacturing: 77% adopted AI in 2024 (up from 70% in 2023), using AI for production (31%), inventory management (28%), customer service (28%), employee training (25%). Lowest adopters: Construction and Agriculture (tied at 1.4% AI usage). AI agent deployment (2025): 62% experimenting, 23% scaling in at least one function — highest in technology, media & telecom, healthcare, and insurance. Only 6-7% are AI high performers (attributing 5%+ of EBIT to AI).
metric_value.unit: Percentage of organizations/respondents, percentage of workers within sectors
metric_value.geographic_scope: Global (McKinsey: 105 countries in 2025 survey; Census data: US-specific)
metric_value.comparison_baseline: 2023: 55% overall AI adoption, 33% GenAI adoption (McKinsey); 2022: ~50% AI adoption hovering for previous 6 years before 2024 spike; Manufacturing: 70% in 2023 vs 77% in 2024; Sales AI usage: 24% in 2023 vs 43% in 2024
metric_value.market_layer: cross-cutting (adoption metric spanning all verticals and market layers; most relevant to application and vertical layers)

trend.trend_direction: Accelerating (adoption broadening rapidly across sectors, GenAI doubling in under a year, but value capture and scaling remain limited)
trend.year_over_year_change: Overall AI adoption: +10pp (78% to 88%, 2024 to 2025); GenAI adoption: +7pp (65% to 72%, 2024 to 2025); From 2023 to 2024: AI adoption surged +17pp (55% to 72%), GenAI nearly doubled (33% to 65%); Manufacturing adoption: +7pp (70% to 77%, 2023 to 2024); Sales AI usage: +19pp (24% to 43%, 2023 to 2024, nearly doubled); Multi-function AI deployment: 68% of organizations now use AI in 2+ functions, 50% in 3+ functions
trend.forecast_value: Gartner: 80%+ of enterprises will have used GenAI APIs or deployed GenAI-enabled applications by 2026; AI agent experimentation at 62% in 2025 suggests agent-based AI will become mainstream by 2026-2027; McKinsey high-performer gap (6% at 5%+ EBIT from AI) likely to widen as leaders scale while laggards remain in pilot mode
trend.velocity_indicator: adoption_doubling_time: GenAI organizational adoption went from 33% (2023) to 65% (early 2024) — doubled in under 12 months; Sales AI adoption doubled from 24% to 43% in one year; Overall AI adoption broke out of 6-year plateau (~50%) to 72% in a single year (2023-2024), then to 88% by mid-2025

entrepreneurial_relevance.relevance_for_entrepreneurs: This is the definitive adoption metric for anyone building AI products or pitching AI-powered startups. Critical implications: (1) At 88% overall adoption, the question is no longer 'will enterprises adopt AI?' but 'how will they capture value?' — the market has moved from evangelism to execution, meaning startup pitches should focus on ROI and implementation, not AI education; (2) The sector breakdown reveals where to sell: Technology, Financial Services/Insurance, and Healthcare are the most AI-mature buyers with established budgets and buying processes — these are the least risky sectors to target. Manufacturing at 77% adoption shows strong traction but with more operational deployment patterns (production, inventory); (3) The massive adoption-to-value gap (88% adopting vs 6% high performers) is the central entrepreneurial opportunity of 2025-2026: most companies are spending on AI but not getting returns, creating demand for solutions that bridge experimentation to production; (4) Construction and Agriculture at 1.4% represent underserved verticals where AI-native startups face less competition but also less buyer sophistication — high risk, high reward; (5) The 43% sales AI adoption rate (doubled in one year) demonstrates how rapidly individual functions can flip from low to high adoption, suggesting timing windows are short for capturing function-specific markets; (6) The AI agent deployment pattern (62% experimenting, 23% scaling) across Technology, Healthcare, and Insurance shows exactly where the next wave of enterprise AI spending will concentrate.
entrepreneurial_relevance.actionable_insight: For go-to-market strategy: target Technology, Financial Services, and Healthcare sectors where adoption is highest and buyers are most educated. For product strategy: build solutions that move companies from 'experimenting' (the 62% with AI agents) to 'scaling' (only 23% today). For pricing: the fact that only 39% see any EBIT impact from AI means founders must lead with concrete ROI metrics. For timing: the sales function's doubling from 24% to 43% in one year shows that functional adoption can move extremely fast — once a vertical tipping point is reached, the window to establish market position is 12-18 months. For underserved markets: Construction and Agriculture's 1.4% adoption represents frontier opportunity for patient founders willing to educate buyers.

confidence.cross_reference: McKinsey's Global Survey on AI is the most widely cited enterprise AI adoption survey globally. Cross-referenced by: Stanford HAI AI Index 2025 (cites McKinsey adoption figures), IBM Global AI Adoption Index, Gartner AI surveys, G2 'Global AI Adoption Statistics' compilation (2017-2025), WalkMe '50 AI Adoption Statistics', Aristek Systems AI statistics compilation, Purdue Business analysis, RSI Security analysis, SwitchSoftware analysis, AIPRM statistics compilation. US Census Bureau data (via St. Louis Fed) provides independent government-collected adoption data. Manufacturing-specific figures cross-referenced with industry surveys. Sales adoption figures corroborated by Salesforce 'State of Sales' reports.
confidence.caveats: All adoption figures are self-reported survey data, not observed behavior — respondents may over-report adoption or conflate experimentation with regular use. The 78% and 88% figures reflect 'at least one business function,' which could mean a single team running a pilot, not organization-wide deployment. McKinsey's respondent base skews toward larger enterprises and McKinsey's professional network, likely under-representing SMEs and less AI-mature organizations. Industry-specific percentages from different sources use different definitions and sample frames (McKinsey global survey vs US Census Bureau vs Salesforce sales-specific surveys), making direct cross-sector comparisons imprecise. The Construction/Agriculture 1.4% figure comes from US Census data, not McKinsey, and measures a different population. Some sector data (e.g., Healthcare, Financial Services) is reported in relative terms ('among the top sectors') rather than precise percentages, limiting quantitative sector-by-sector comparison. GDP-weighting of McKinsey survey adjusts for geographic representation but may introduce other biases.
